Capacity-Constrained Online Convex Optimization
with Delayed Feedback

Alexander Ryabchenko ††thanks: Department of Statistical Sciences, University of Toronto; Vector Institute. Email: alex.rbch.research@gmail.com.    Idan Attias ††thanks: Institute for Data, Econometrics, Algorithms, and Learning (IDEAL), hosted by UIC and TTIC. Email: idanattias88@gmail.com.    Daniel M. Roy ††thanks: Department of Statistical Sciences, University of Toronto; Vector Institute. Email: daniel.roy@utoronto.ca.
Abstract

Online learning with delayed feedback typically assumes that the learner can track all pending rounds until their feedback arrives. In practice, tracking resources are finite, and feedback from untracked rounds is permanently lost. In this paper, we study delayed online convex optimization (OCO) under a hard capacity constraint, where at most CC pending rounds can be tracked at any time. To model delay information, we introduce a semi-clairvoyant model that refines the clairvoyant assumption from prior work: rather than requiring delays to be known at prediction time, the learner observes delay expirations online, consistent with the classical unconstrained delayed setting. Our approach proceeds via a reduction to a novel “delayed and weighted” OCO problem, using a scheduler that randomizes tracking decisions and importance-weights the resulting observations. For this base problem, we propose and analyze Delayed-Weighted FTRL and its bandit analogue, establishing regret bounds that explicitly characterize the interaction between time-varying weights and delayed feedback. Combining these base learners with our schedulers yields the first regret guarantees for capacity-constrained OCO under convex and strongly convex losses, for both first-order and bandit feedback. For first-order feedback, capacity C=Ω⁡(log⁡T)C=\Omega(\log T) suffices to recover standard delayed OCO rates up to logarithmic factors. For bandit feedback, the regret rates are modulated by powers of (1+σmax/C)(1+\sigma_{\text{max}}/C), where σmax\sigma_{\text{max}} is the maximum number of pending observations at any time. This allows the regret bound to degrade gracefully when C<σmaxC<\sigma_{\text{max}}, while remaining sublinear.

1 Introduction

Online convex optimization is a canonical framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty [18, 34]: a player repeatedly selects an action from a convex domain, incurs a convex loss, and receives either full gradient information (first-order feedback) or only the incurred scalar loss (bandit feedback). We refer to these two settings as Online Convex Optimization (OCO) and Bandit Convex Optimization (BCO), respectively. A long line of work studies delayed feedback in OCO and BCO, as well as in sequential decision-making more broadly, where the observation from round tt arrives only at round t+dtt+d_{t} [21, 38, 9]. The vast majority of this literature, however, takes for granted that the player has unlimited capacity to track pending rounds, that is, every outstanding feedback will eventually be observed, regardless of how many are pending simultaneously.

In many practical settings, only a limited number of rounds can be tracked concurrently. A natural example arises in clinical trials: a study can actively monitor only a bounded number of patients at any given time, and outcomes are observed only for the patients selected for monitoring — side effects may still manifest in unmonitored patients, but the trial never observes them. [39] formalized this limitation as a hard capacity constraint, capping the number of tracked rounds by a capacity parameter CC, and studied it in the multi-armed bandit setting.

This paper extends the capacity-constrained framework from finite-action settings to convex domains, deriving regret bounds for both OCO and BCO with explicit dependence on the capacity CC. The bandit setting is substantially more challenging even without delays or capacity constraints, as the player must optimize over a continuous domain from scalar loss observations alone. Moreover, we relax the clairvoyant delay model of prior work, which assumes delays are known at prediction time; our framework instead reveals delays only upon their expiration, matching the information available in standard delayed online learning. This information structure is also closer to the standard clairvoyant model in online job scheduling (e.g., [6]): a job’s processing time is revealed upon arrival, but the number of future jobs arriving during its processing interval is unknown in advance.

Contributions.

Following the reduction approach of [39], we decompose capacity-constrained delayed OCO into two components: a scheduler, which randomly selects the rounds to track subject to the capacity constraint, and a base learner, which receives the resulting feedback stream with importance weights correcting for untracked rounds. Extending this reduction to convex domains introduces two new challenges: first, designing OCO and BCO algorithms that can accommodate feedback that is simultaneously delayed and non-uniformly weighted; and second, controlling the stochastic weight process induced by the scheduler in the presence of convex losses and bandit gradient estimation. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    Delayed-weighted OCO and BCO (Section 3). We introduce OCO and BCO with feedback that is simultaneously delayed and weighted, extending the scale-free online learning framework of [33] to delayed feedback. We analyze a delayed-weighted variant of Follow-the-Regularized-Leader and its bandit analogue, obtaining regret bounds that identify pairwise interactions between weights of rounds with overlapping delays as the structural cost of combining weighting with delays. These results are new for convex domains and may be of independent interest. This framework forms the base problem to which we reduce the capacity-constrained setting.

  • •

    Unified proxy-delay scheduling (Section 4). To handle delays that are unknown at prediction time, [39] introduced the idea of sampling proxy delays as surrogates for the true delays. We unify such constructions into a general framework parameterized by proxy-delay distributions, and introduce a new scheduler calibrated to the maximum number of pending observations, σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}, that yields uniform importance weights, a property crucial for our strongly convex and bandit guarantees. Importantly, the algorithm does not require prior knowledge of σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}, as it can be removed via the doubling trick (Appendix F).

  • •

    Capacity-dependent regret bounds (Section 5). Combining the delayed-weighted regret bounds with the proxy-delay schedulers yields regret guarantees for capacity-constrained OCO and BCO; see Table 1.

    For first-order feedback, capacity C=Ω⁡(log⁡T)C=\Omega(\log T) suffices to match the optimal unconstrained rates in terms of the total delay dtotd_{\textnormal{tot}} and the maximum number of pending observations σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}, up to logarithmic factors, since σmax≤2​dtot\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\leq\sqrt{2d_{\textnormal{tot}}}. For bandit feedback in dimension kk, the capacity constraint enters the dimension-dependent terms through factors of (1+σmax/C)1/4(1+\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}/C)^{1/4} in the convex case and (1+σmax/C)1/3(1+\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}/C)^{1/3} in the strongly convex case, so the bounds degrade gracefully as capacity decreases. The delay-dependent terms match the optimal σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}} scaling of [40] in the strongly convex case; for convex losses they scale as T​σmax\sqrt{T\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}} rather than dtot\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}, but still improve over the T​dmax\sqrt{Td_{\textnormal{max}}} dependence of [48], since σmax≤dmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\leq d_{\textnormal{max}}. The regime σmax≪dmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\ll d_{\textnormal{max}} is particularly natural in queueing systems: σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}} captures peak concurrency (e.g., [28]), while dmaxd_{\textnormal{max}} is driven by the tail of the service-time distribution, which can produce extreme outliers even when the average service time is moderate.

Remark 1.1 (Extensions)

Our framework allows the player to preempt tracked rounds—that is, to stop tracking them before their feedback arrives. There is also a non-preemptive variant of the problem, in which once a round is tracked, it cannot be dropped until its feedback is delivered. Several of our schedulers are non-preemptive by construction and achieve analogous guarantees in this setting; see Appendix G. Additionally, the same guarantees extend to the fully non-clairvoyant setting, where delays dtd_{t} are revealed only at times t+dtt+d_{t} for rounds whose feedback is observed, provided that sufficient information about delay-related quantities such as dtotd_{\textnormal{tot}} or σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}} is available for tuning the algorithm parameters.

Related work.

The capacity-constrained framework was introduced by [39] for experts and multi-armed bandits; this work extends it to OCO and BCO. Delayed online learning traces back to [50], whose subsampling argument for fixed delays dt=d0d_{t}=d_{0} implies minimax rates of order Θ⁡(T⁡(d0+1))\Theta(\sqrt{T(d_{0}+1)}) and Θ⁡((d0+1)​ln⁡T)\Theta((d_{0}+1)\ln T) when applied to non-delayed problems with square-root and logarithmic regret, respectively. These fixed-delay rates imply Ω⁡(dtot+T)\Omega(\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}+T}) and Ω⁡((σmax+1)​ln⁡T)\Omega((\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}+1)\ln T) lower bounds for arbitrary delays under convex and strongly convex losses, respectively. Matching upper bounds for first-order OCO were obtained by [38, 22, 14] for convex losses and by [36] for strongly convex losses; earlier, [47] achieved the rate O⁡(dmax​ln⁡T)O(d_{\textnormal{max}}\ln T). Delayed BCO was initiated by [19] and refined by [5, 48]. A unified view via reduction to non-delayed OCO appears in [40], achieving optimal delay-dependent terms with respect to σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}} and dtotd_{\textnormal{tot}}. Beyond OCO, delayed feedback has been studied in adversarial bandits [9, 44, 53], MDPs [23, 20], and combinatorial settings [45]. For additional related work, see Appendix A.

2 Problem Setting and Notation

Let T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N} denote the time horizon, and let 𝒦⊂ℝk\mathcal{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^{k} be a non-empty, convex, and closed domain of dimension k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, equipped with a norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| and its dual norm ∥⋅∥⋆\|\cdot\|_{\star}.

We study a TT-round game between a player and an adversary with delayed, capacity-constrained feedback (Figure 1). Before the game begins, the adversary fixes a sequence of convex, differentiable losses ft:𝒦→ℝf_{t}:\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{R} and delays dt∈{0,…,T−t}d_{t}\in\{0,\ldots,T-t\} for t∈[T]t\in[T].11 1 The restriction dt≤T−td_{t}\leq T-t is without loss of generality: feedback arriving after round TT cannot affect any prediction. At each round tt, the player selects xt∈𝒦x_{t}\in\mathcal{K} and incurs the (unobserved) loss ft​(xt)f_{t}(x_{t}). The corresponding feedback—∇ft​(xt)\nabla f_{t}(x_{t}) in the first-order model or ft​(xt)f_{t}(x_{t}) in the bandit model—arrives only at the end of round t+dtt+d_{t}, and is observed if and only if tt belongs at that time to a tracking set 𝒮⊆[T]\mathcal{S}\subseteq[T] of maximum size C∈ℕC\in\mathbb{N} (the capacity), maintained by the player throughout the game. At the start of each round, the player may preempt (i.e., remove from 𝒮\mathcal{S}) any subset of round indices, irrevocably discarding their pending feedback; they may then add the current round’s index to 𝒮\mathcal{S}, subject to the capacity constraint. If C≥TC\geq T, then the learner observes all delayed feedback, recovering the standard delayed-feedback setting. The goal is to achieve strong performance while maintaining a tracking set of sublinear size.

We consider two natural frameworks for capacity-constrained delayed feedback, which differ in how the delay sequence is revealed to the player. In the clairvoyant framework, dtd_{t} is revealed to the player at the start of round tt. In the semi-clairvoyant framework, the player learns dtd_{t} only at round t+dtt+d_{t}: if t∈𝒮t\in\mathcal{S}, the player receives indexed feedback for round tt, (t,∇ft​(xt))(t,\nabla f_{t}(x_{t})) or (t,ft​(xt))(t,f_{t}(x_{t})); otherwise, the player receives an empty acknowledgment (t,⟂)(t,\perp), from which dtd_{t} can be inferred as the elapsed time since round tt. Semi-clairvoyance thus preserves exactly the delay information available at runtime in standard delayed online learning; the capacity constraint restricts only the content of the feedback, not the player’s knowledge of when feedback would have arrived.

The regret against a comparator u∈𝒦u\in\mathcal{K} is defined as RT​(u)=∑t=1T(ft​(xt)−ft​(u))R_{T}(u)=\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}(f_{t}(x_{t})-f_{t}(u)), and its expected regret as R¯T​(u)=𝔼⁡[RT​(u)]\widebar{R}_{T}(u)=\E[R_{T}(u)]. Letting x∗∈arg​minx∈𝒦∑t=1Tft(x)x^{*}\in\operatornamewithlimits{arg\,min}_{x\in\mathcal{K}}\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(x) denote the best action in hindsight, the objective is to minimize RT​(x∗)R_{T}(x^{*}) almost surely or its expectation R¯T​(x∗)\widebar{R}_{T}(x^{*}).

Regularity assumptions.

We impose the following standard regularity assumptions, which are necessary to obtain sublinear regret guarantees in online convex optimization.

Assumption 2.1

The diameter of 𝒦\mathcal{K} is bounded by DD, i.e., supx,y∈𝒦‖x−y‖≤D\sup_{x,y\in\mathcal{K}}\|x-y\|\leq D.

Assumption 2.2

For all t∈[T]t\in[T], ftf_{t} has its gradient norm bounded by GG, i.e., supx∈𝒦‖∇ft​(x)‖⋆≤G\sup_{x\in\mathcal{K}}\|\nabla f_{t}(x)\|_{\star}\!\leq\!G.

Assumptions 2.1 and 2.2 hold throughout the paper. When deriving stronger guarantees, we also impose the following strong convexity condition, stated explicitly when invoked.

Assumption 2.3

For all t∈[T]t\in[T], ftf_{t} is λ\lambda-strongly convex for λ>0\lambda>0, i.e., for all x,y∈𝒦x,y\in\mathcal{K},

ft​(y)≥ft​(x)+⟨∇ft​(x),y−x⟩+λ2​‖y−x‖2.f_{t}(y)\geq f_{t}(x)+\langle{\nabla f_{t}(x),\,y-x}\rangle+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|y-x\|^{2}.

For BCO, we take ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| to be the Euclidean norm ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} and impose two additional assumptions.

Assumption 2.4

For all t∈[T]t\in[T], absolute values of ftf_{t} are bounded by MM, i.e., supx∈𝒦|ft​(x)|≤M\sup_{x\in\mathcal{K}}|f_{t}(x)|\!\leq\!M.

Assumption 2.5

The domain satisfies r​𝔹k⊆𝒦⊆R​𝔹kr\mathbb{B}^{k}\subseteq\mathcal{K}\subseteq R\mathbb{B}^{k} for some radii 0<r<R0<r<R.

Notation.

For n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, we let [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}. For any sequence (at)t=1T(\mathrm{a}_{t})_{t=1}^{T}, indexed over [T][T], we write atot=∑t=1Tat\mathrm{a}_{\textnormal{tot}}=\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathrm{a}_{t} and amax=maxt∈[T]⁡at\mathrm{a}_{\textnormal{max}}=\max_{t\in[T]}\mathrm{a}_{t}. We denote by 𝔹k\mathbb{B}^{k} and 𝕊k−1\mathbb{S}^{k-1} the unit Euclidean ball and sphere centered at the origin in ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k}, respectively. For any S⊆ℝkS\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{k} and c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, we let c​S={c​x:x∈S}cS=\{cx:x\in S\}.

2.1 Notation for Delays and the Tracking Set

The interplay between delays and the capacity constraint requires keeping careful track of which past rounds have produced feedback, which are still pending, and which the player is currently tracking. We introduce this notation and present a few standard identities in delayed online learning.

Observed and backlog sets.

At the start of each round t∈[T]t\in[T], the past rounds split into those whose feedback has already arrived and those whose feedback is still pending. We denote these by

𝒪t={s∈[t−1]:s+ds<t},ℬt={s∈[t−1]:t≤s+ds},\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{t}\;=\;\{s\in[t-1]:s+d_{s}<t\},\qquad\mathcal{B}_{t}\;=\;\{s\in[t-1]:t\leq s+d_{s}\},

respectively; together they partition the past, 𝒪t∪ℬt=[t−1]\mathcal{O}_{t}\cup\mathcal{B}_{t}=[t-1] and 𝒪t∩ℬt=∅\mathcal{O}_{t}\cap\mathcal{B}_{t}=\emptyset. We write σt=|ℬt|\sigma_{t}=|\mathcal{B}_{t}| for the backlog set size (or just backlog) at round tt, and define

σmax=maxt∈[T]⁡σt,dmax=maxt∈[T]⁡dt,dtot=∑t=1Tdt,\textstyle\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\;=\;\max_{t\in[T]}\sigma_{t},\qquad d_{\textnormal{max}}\;=\;\max_{t\in[T]}d_{t},\qquad d_{\textnormal{tot}}\;=\;\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_{t},

the maximum backlog, maximum delay, and total delay over the game. The next lemma collects two identities relating these quantities, which we will use repeatedly to bound the cost of the backlog.

Lemma 2.6 (Backlog properties)

For any delays (dt)t=1T(d_{t})_{t=1}^{T} with dt∈{0,…,T−t}d_{t}\in\{0,\ldots,T-t\}, the following hold:

∑t=1Tσt=dtotandσmax≤min⁡{2​dtot,dmax}.\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sigma_{t}=d_{\textnormal{tot}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\leq\min\{\sqrt{2d_{\textnormal{tot}}},\,d_{\textnormal{max}}\}.

The first identity is the standard average-case quantity governing regret in delayed online learning [9]; the second controls the worst-case backlog.

Tracking set evolution.

Among the pending rounds, the player tracks only a subset. To reason about which rounds are tracked at each point in time, we consider the post-preemption snapshot

𝒮t={s∈[T]:s lies in 𝒮 immediately after preemption in round t}.\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{t}\;=\;\left\{s\in[T]:\text{$s$ lies in $\mathcal{S}$ immediately after preemption in round $t$}\right\}.

It satisfies 𝒮t⊆ℬt\mathcal{S}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{B}_{t}, |𝒮t|≤C|\mathcal{S}_{t}|\leq C, and 𝒮t+1⊆𝒮t∪{t}\mathcal{S}_{t+1}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{t}\cup\{t\}. The first inclusion holds because every round in 𝒮\mathcal{S} has been played but has not yet delivered feedback and round tt itself has not yet been added at this point. The second is the capacity constraint. The third reflects that between round tt and round t+1t+1, the set may only gain index tt (if added) and may only lose indices (through feedback or preemption).

2.2 Notation for Bandit Feedback and Smoothing

The bandit setting requires constructing gradient estimates from function values alone. We follow the standard single-point approach of [15], which replaces each loss function with a smoothed surrogate whose gradient admits an unbiased estimator from a single bandit query.

Smoothing.

Under Assumption 2.5, the inclusion r​𝔹k⊆𝒦r\mathbb{B}^{k}\subseteq\mathcal{K} implies (1−δ/r)​𝒦+δ​𝔹k⊆𝒦(1-\delta/r)\,\mathcal{K}+\delta\,\mathbb{B}^{k}\subseteq\mathcal{K} for all δ∈(0,r]\delta\in(0,r], and so any point of the shrunken domain (1−δ/r)​𝒦(1-\delta/r)\mathcal{K} admits a δ\delta-ball of perturbations that stays in 𝒦\mathcal{K}. For such δ\delta and any integrable f:𝒦→ℝf:\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{R}, we define the δ\delta-smoothing of ff as

fδ:(1−δ/r)​𝒦→ℝ,fδ​(x)=𝔼v∼Unif​(𝔹k)⁡[f⁡(x+δ​v)].f^{\delta}:(1-\delta/r)\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{R},\qquad f^{\delta}(x)\;=\;\E_{v\sim\textnormal{Unif}(\mathbb{B}^{k})}\bigl[f(x+\delta v)\bigr].

The key properties of fδf^{\delta} are summarized in the following theorem.

2.7[15]

For any δ∈(0,r]\delta\in(0,r] and integrable f:𝒦→ℝf:\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{R}:

  1. 1.

    The δ\delta-smoothing fδf^{\delta} is differentiable with gradients ∇fδ​(x)=kδ​𝔼u∼Unif​(𝕊k−1)​[f⁡(x+δ​u)​u]\nabla f^{\delta}(x)=\tfrac{k}{\delta}\E_{u\sim\textnormal{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{k-1})}[f(x+\delta u)\,u].

  2. 2.

    If ff is convex (λ\lambda-strongly convex), so is fδf^{\delta}.

  3. 3.

    If ff is GG-Lipschitz, then |fδ​(x)−f⁡(x)|≤G​δ|f^{\delta}(x)-f(x)|\leq G\delta and ‖∇fδ​(x)‖≤G\|\nabla f^{\delta}(x)\|\leq G for x∈(1−δ/r)​𝒦x\in(1-\delta/r)\mathcal{K}.

The first item underpins single-point gradient estimation; the remaining two ensure that fδf^{\delta} preserves the regularity of ff and stays uniformly close to it.

3 Online Convex Optimization with Delayed and Weighted Feedback

This section introduces a weighted variant of OCO with delayed feedback (Figure 2) that serves as the foundation for the reductions in subsequent sections. The game itself involves no tracking set management; the connection to capacity-constrained OCO emerges only through the reductions. Beyond its role in our reductions, this game gives, to our knowledge, the first treatment of scale-free online convex optimization [33] under delayed feedback.

In this game, the adversary fixes losses ft:𝒦→ℝf_{t}:\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{R}, delays dt∈{0,…,T−t}d_{t}\in\{0,\ldots,T-t\}, and weights wt≥0w_{t}\geq 0 in advance. At each round tt, the player predicts xt∈𝒦x_{t}\in\mathcal{K} and incurs the weighted loss wt​ft​(xt)w_{t}f_{t}(x_{t}). The feedback for round tt is revealed at the end of round t+dtt+d_{t}, together with the weight wtw_{t}.

We measure performance through the weighted regret against a comparator u∈𝒦u\in\mathcal{K},

RTw​(u)=∑t=1Twt​(ft​(xt)−ft​(u)),\displaystyle R^{w}_{T}(u)\;=\;\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}\bigl(f_{t}(x_{t})-f_{t}(u)\bigr),

and its expectation R¯Tw​(u)=𝔼⁡[RTw​(u)]\widebar{R}_{T}^{w}(u)=\E[R_{T}^{w}(u)]. The resulting problem is not equivalent to delayed OCO on the rescaled losses ft′​(x)=wt​ft​(x)f_{t}^{\prime}(x)=w_{t}f_{t}(x): since the weights wtw_{t} may vary widely, this vacuous rescaling yields bounds scaling with maxt⁡wt\max_{t}w_{t}, whereas we require finer weight dependence for the capacity-constrained analysis.

We now produce algorithms for this delayed and weighted game in both first-order and bandit feedback models following the delayed-update paradigm of [14]: at each round, the learner applies an update based on all feedback items that arrive in that round, with the modification that each item is now scaled by its weight wsw_{s}. Section 3.1 develops this for first-order feedback, yielding a weighted variant of Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (FTRL). Section 3.2 extends the construction to bandit feedback using the single-point estimator of [15] and prediction drift control techniques from [40].

3.1 First-Order Feedback: DW-FTRL

Given a non-increasing learning-rate sequence (ηt)t=1T⊂(0,∞)(\eta_{t})_{t=1}^{T}\subset(0,\infty), define the regularization increments α1=1/η1\alpha_{1}=1/\eta_{1} and αt=1/ηt−1/ηt−1\alpha_{t}=1/\eta_{t}-1/\eta_{t-1}. Starting from x1∈𝒦x_{1}\in\mathcal{K}, delayed-weighted FTRL (DW-FTRL) updates are given by

DW-FTRL:xt+1\displaystyle\makebox[50.00008pt][c]{\text{DW-FTRL:}}\quad x_{t+1} =arg​minx∈𝒦⟨x,∑s∈𝒪t+1ws∇fs(xs)⟩+∑s=1tαs2∥xs−x∥2.\displaystyle=\operatornamewithlimits{arg\,min}_{x\in\mathcal{K}}\,\langle{x,\textstyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{O}_{t+1}}w_{s}\nabla f_{s}(x_{s})}\rangle+\textstyle\sum_{s=1}^{t}\frac{\alpha_{s}}{2}\,\|x_{s}\!-\!x\|^{2}. (1)

Each update aggregates the weighted gradients revealed so far and regularizes against the running sequence of iterates. The following theorem bounds the weighted regret of DW-FTRL.

3.1

For all u∈𝒦u\in\mathcal{K}, predictions (xt)t=1T(x_{t})_{t=1}^{T} generated by DW-FTRL (1) satisfy

RTw​(u)≤D22​ηT+G2​∑t=1Tηt−1​(wt2+wt​∑s∈ℬtws),\displaystyle R^{w}_{T}(u)\leq\tfrac{D^{2}}{2\eta_{T}}+G^{2}\,\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t-1}(w_{t}^{2}+w_{t}\textstyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}w_{s}),

where η0=η1\eta_{0}=\eta_{1}. Moreover, under λ\lambda-strong convexity (2.3),

RTw​(u)≤∑t=1Tαt−wt​λ2​‖xt−u‖2+G2​∑t=1Tηt−1​(wt2+wt​∑s∈ℬtws).\displaystyle R^{w}_{T}(u)\leq\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\tfrac{\alpha_{t}-w_{t}\lambda}{2}\,\|x_{t}-u\|^{2}+G^{2}\,\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t-1}(w_{t}^{2}+w_{t}\textstyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}w_{s}).

In the delayed FTRL bounds of Theorem 3.1, weighting manifests through pairwise interactions wt​wsw_{t}w_{s} for every pair of rounds t,st,s such that s∈ℬts\in\mathcal{B}_{t}, i.e., the feedback of ss is still pending at round tt. Without delays the backlog set is empty and only the diagonal terms wt2w_{t}^{2} remain, recovering the standard weighted FTRL bounds from scale-free online learning [33]. Conversely, setting weights to wt=1w_{t}=1 recovers standard delayed FTRL bounds [36].

3.2 Bandit Feedback: DW-FTBL

We extend the delayed-weighted updates to bandit feedback through the classical center-perturbation construction applied to a non-increasing sequence of smoothing parameters (δt)t=1T⊂(0,r](\delta_{t})_{t=1}^{T}\subset(0,r]. Each round we sample a direction ut∼Unif​(𝕊k−1)u_{t}\sim\textnormal{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{k-1}) and pick some σ⁡(u1,…,ut−1)\sigma(u_{1},\ldots,u_{t-1})-measurable center yt∈𝒦y_{t}\in\mathcal{K} to play the perturbed point

xt=(1−δt/r)​yt+δt​ut,\displaystyle x_{t}\;=\;(1-\delta_{t}/r)\,y_{t}+\delta_{t}\,u_{t},

which lies in 𝒦\mathcal{K} for δt≤r\delta_{t}\leq r due to Assumption 2.5. Letting ℱt=σ⁡(u1,…,ut−1)\mathcal{F}_{t}=\sigma(u_{1},\ldots,u_{t-1}), the sequence of centers yty_{t} is ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-measurable while the predictions xtx_{t} are ℱt+1\mathcal{F}_{t+1}-measurable. By Theorem 2.7, the bandit feedback ft​(xt)f_{t}(x_{t}) yields the single-point estimator

g^t=kδt​ft​(xt)​utsuch that𝔼⁡[g^t∣ℱt]=∇ftδt​((1−δt/r)​yt).\displaystyle\widehat{g}_{t}\;=\;\tfrac{k}{\delta_{t}}\,f_{t}(x_{t})\,u_{t}\quad\text{such that}\quad\E[\widehat{g}_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]\;=\;\nabla f_{t}^{\delta_{t}}\bigl((1-\delta_{t}/r)\,y_{t}\bigr).

It remains to specify the ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-measurable centers (yt)t=1T(y_{t})_{t=1}^{T}. Given a non-increasing learning-rate sequence (ηt)t=1T(\eta_{t})_{t=1}^{T} with regularization increments (αt)t=1T(\alpha_{t})_{t=1}^{T} as in Section 3.1, starting from y1∈𝒦y_{1}\in\mathcal{K}, we define the delayed-weighted Follow-The-Bandit-Leader (DW-FTBL) updates by

DW-FTBL:yt+1\displaystyle\makebox[50.00008pt][c]{\text{DW-FTBL:}}\quad y_{t+1} =arg​miny∈𝒦⁡⟨y,∑s∈𝒪t+1ws​g^s⟩+∑s=1tαs2​‖ys−y‖2.\displaystyle=\operatornamewithlimits{arg\,min}_{y\in\mathcal{K}}\,\langle{y,\,\textstyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{O}_{t+1}}w_{s}\,\widehat{g}_{s}}\rangle+\textstyle\sum_{s=1}^{t}\tfrac{\alpha_{s}}{2}\,\|y_{s}-y\|^{2}. (2)

This is the bandit analog of DW-FTRL (1), with the weighted estimators ws​g^sw_{s}\,\widehat{g}_{s} in place of the weighted gradients ws∇fs(xs)w_{s}\,\nabla f_{s}(x_{s}). Since each g^s\widehat{g}_{s} is ℱs+1\mathcal{F}_{s+1}-measurable, the resulting centers (yt)t=1T(y_{t})_{t=1}^{T} are indeed ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-adapted. The next theorem bounds the expected regret of both updates.

3.2

For all u∈𝒦u\in\mathcal{K}, predictions (xt)t=1T(x_{t})_{t=1}^{T} generated by DW-FTBL (2) satisfy

R¯Tw​(u)\displaystyle\widebar{R}^{w}_{T}(u) ≤D22​ηT+2​G2​∑t=1Tηt−1​(k2​M2​wt2G2​δt2+k​M​wtG​δt​∑s∈ℬtws2+wt​∑s∈ℬtws)+3​G​Dr​∑t=1Twt​δt,\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{D^{2}}{2\eta_{T}}+2G^{2}\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\!\eta_{t-1}\!\left(\tfrac{k^{2}M^{2}w_{t}^{2}}{G^{2}\delta_{t}^{2}}+\tfrac{kMw_{t}}{G\delta_{t}}\sqrt{\textstyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}w_{s}^{2}}+w_{t}\textstyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}w_{s}\right)+\tfrac{3GD}{r}\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}\delta_{t},

where η0=η1\eta_{0}=\eta_{1}. Moreover, under λ\lambda-strong convexity (2.3),

R¯Tw​(u)\displaystyle\widebar{R}^{w}_{T}(u) ≤𝔼⁡[∑t=1Tαt−wt​λ2​‖yt−u‖2]\displaystyle\leq\E\!\left[\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\tfrac{\alpha_{t}-w_{t}\lambda}{2}\|y_{t}-u\|^{2}\right]
+2G2∑t=1Tηt−1(k2​M2​wt2G2​δt2+k​M​wtG​δt∑s∈ℬtws2+wt∑s∈ℬtws)+10​G2λ​r∑t=1Twtδt.\displaystyle+2G^{2}\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t-1}\!\left(\tfrac{k^{2}M^{2}w_{t}^{2}}{G^{2}\delta_{t}^{2}}+\tfrac{kMw_{t}}{G\delta_{t}}\sqrt{\textstyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}w_{s}^{2}}+w_{t}\textstyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}w_{s}\right)+\tfrac{10G^{2}}{\lambda r}\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}\delta_{t}.

Compared to Theorem 3.1, weighting has a more severe effect under bandit feedback. Beyond the interaction wt​∑s∈ℬtwsw_{t}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}w_{s}, the bound carries an additional cross term k​M​wtG​δt​(∑s∈ℬtws2)1/2\tfrac{kMw_{t}}{G\delta_{t}}(\textstyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}w_{s}^{2})^{1/2}, through which the variance of pending gradient estimators accumulates in ℓ2\ell^{2} rather than ℓ1\ell^{1}. For uniform weights wt≡ww_{t}\equiv w, AM-GM absorbs this term into its neighbors, recovering the delayed bandit rate of [40] for w=1w=1. With non-uniform weights, the (∑s∈ℬtws2)1/2(\textstyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}w_{s}^{2})^{1/2} factor introduces an ℓ2\ell^{2} dependence that has no counterpart in the first-order setting.

4 Reduction via Proxy Delay Scheduling

We now reduce capacity-constrained OCO with delayed feedback (Figure 1) to delayed-weighted OCO from the previous section (Figure 2). For concreteness, we present this reduction under the semi-clairvoyant framework (i.e., the delay is not known at prediction time), but it also applies to the clairvoyant and non-clairvoyant frameworks; see Remark 4.2. The reduction is implemented by a wrapper 𝒲⁡(𝒜,𝔇)\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{A},\mathfrak{D}) (Algorithm 1) that takes as input an algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} for delayed and weighted OCO and is parameterized by a sequence of proxy delay distributions 𝔇=(𝔇t)t=1T\mathfrak{D}=(\mathfrak{D}_{t})_{t=1}^{T}. These distributions govern how the wrapper maintains the tracking set, as described below.

Proxy delay scheduling.

The distributions 𝔇\mathfrak{D} are used to sample proxy delays dt′∼𝔇td^{\prime}_{t}\sim\mathfrak{D}_{t} on ℤ≥−1∪{∞}\mathbb{Z}_{\geq-1}\cup\{\infty\} at each round tt, determining round tt’s lifetime in the tracking set: round tt is added to 𝒮\mathcal{S} only if dt′≥0d^{\prime}_{t}\geq 0 and 𝒮\mathcal{S} is not full, and is preempted from 𝒮\mathcal{S} at round t+dt′+1t+d^{\prime}_{t}+1 if its feedback has not arrived by then. Feedback from round tt is therefore observed if and only if the proxy delay covers the true delay (i.e., dt′≥dtd^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t}) and the tracking set was not full when round tt was considered for admission (i.e., |𝒮t|<C|\mathcal{S}_{t}|<C). The choice of 𝔇\mathfrak{D} navigates a fundamental tradeoff: heavier-tailed distributions are more likely to cover true delays but keep rounds in 𝒮\mathcal{S} longer, risking saturation.

Algorithm overview.

The wrapper treats a base algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} for OCO with delayed and weighted feedback as a black box and feeds it a simulated feedback stream constructed from the observations available in the original capacity-constrained problem. Using 𝔇\mathfrak{D}, the weights are set as importance-weighted indicators of whether the corresponding feedback is observed.

Every round tt, the wrapper outputs 𝒜\mathcal{A}’s prediction xtx_{t} as its own. The feedback-handling step is summarized in Figure 3. At round s+dss+d_{s}, if ss is still in 𝒮\mathcal{S} the wrapper forwards (s,ws,vs)(s,w_{s},v_{s}) to 𝒜\mathcal{A} with importance weight ws=1/ℙ⁡(ds′≥ds)w_{s}=1/\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{s}\geq d_{s}) and observation vs∈{∇fs​(xs),fs​(xs)}v_{s}\in\{\nabla f_{s}(x_{s}),\,f_{s}(x_{s})\}; otherwise it forwards the zero placeholder (s,0,0)(s,0,0). The next theorem records the key properties of the random weights and reduces the wrapper’s regret to the weighted regret of 𝒜\mathcal{A} plus a saturation penalty for 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

4.1Regret of Algorithm 1

The weights forwarded to 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfy

wt=𝕀⁡(|𝒮t|<C)​𝕀​(dt′≥dt)ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt),𝔼⁡[wt]≤1,𝔼⁡[wt2]≤1ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt),𝔼⁡[wt​ws]≤1,w_{t}=\tfrac{\mathbb{I}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|<C)\,\mathbb{I}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})}{\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})},\quad\E[w_{t}]\leq 1,\quad\E[w_{t}^{2}]\leq\tfrac{1}{\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})},\quad\E[w_{t}w_{s}]\leq 1,

for all distinct t,s∈[T]t,s\in[T]. Moreover, the expected regret satisfies

R¯T​(u)≤𝔼⁡[∑t=1Twt​(ft​(xt)−ft​(u))]+GD​∑t=1Tℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C).\widebar{R}_{T}(u)\;\leq\;\E\!\left[\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}\bigl(f_{t}(x_{t})-f_{t}(u)\bigr)\right]+GD\,\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{P}\bigl(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C\bigr).

Theorem 4.1 reduces the analysis of capacity-constrained OCO to bounding two quantities: the weighted regret of 𝒜\mathcal{A} (Theorem 3.1 or 3.2) and the saturation probabilities ℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C). The choice of 𝔇t\mathfrak{D}_{t} navigates the tradeoff between them; we provide concrete instantiations of proxy delay distributions in the next section.

Remark 4.2 (Applicability across frameworks)

Beyond the semi-clairvoyant framework, this reduction immediately extends to the clairvoyant framework, since the player can simulate the semi-clairvoyant empty acknowledgments from known delays. It also extends to the non-clairvoyant framework provided that 𝒜\mathcal{A} ignores zero-weight observations, i.e., its predictions are unchanged when a zero-weight item is forwarded; the wrapper can then simply skip the forwarding step for untracked rounds. The algorithms of Section 3 satisfy this property, since a zero weight zeroes out the corresponding gradient term in the update.

4.1 Concrete Proxy Distributions

We now give concrete choices of proxy distributions 𝔇\mathfrak{D}. Lemma 4.3 states a generic sufficient condition under which the tracking set saturates with probability at most exp⁡(−C)\exp(-C), and the two corollaries instantiate this condition for specific families of 𝔇t\mathfrak{D}_{t}. The first scheduler, an adaptation of the Pareto-based construction of [39], sets the per-round observation probability ptp_{t} inversely proportional to the delay dtd_{t}. The second is new to this work: it sets a uniform per-round observation probability pp inversely proportional to the maximum backlog σmax=maxt⁡|ℬt|\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}=\max_{t}|\mathcal{B}_{t}| (Section 2.1), trading adaptivity for a constant weight scale 1/p1/p across rounds, which is essential for the bounds we obtain in the strongly convex and bandit settings. This scheduler requires knowledge of σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}; however, the resulting regret bounds in Section 5 can nevertheless be extended to unknown σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}} via a novel doubling trick in Appendix F.

Lemma 4.3

Suppose the proxy delay distributions 𝔇=(𝔇t)t=1T\mathfrak{D}=(\mathfrak{D}_{t})_{t=1}^{T} from Algorithm 1 satisfy

∑s∈ℬt∪{t}ℙ⁡(ds′≥t−s)≤C8for every ​t∈[T].\textstyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}\cup\{t\}}\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{s}\geq t-s)\;\leq\;\tfrac{C}{8}\qquad\text{for every }t\in[T].

Then ℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)≤exp⁡(−C)\mathbb{P}\bigl(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C\bigr)\leq\exp(-C) for every t∈[T]t\in[T].

The bound follows immediately from a Chernoff inequality on the size of 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t}.

Corollary 4.4 (Pareto scheduler)

For each t∈[T]t\in[T], let Ht=∑j=1t1jH_{t}=\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{t}\tfrac{1}{j}. Let 𝔇t\mathfrak{D}_{t} be the shifted Pareto distribution 22 2 A Pareto​(xm,α)\textnormal{Pareto}(x_{m},\alpha) random variable has tail CDF ℙ⁡(X≥x)=min⁡{1,(xm/x)α}\mathbb{P}(X\geq x)=\min\{1,\,(x_{m}/x)^{\alpha}\} for x>0x>0.

𝔇t=⌊Pareto​(C16​Ht, 1)⌋−1.\mathfrak{D}_{t}\;=\;\lfloor\textnormal{Pareto}\bigl(\tfrac{C}{16H_{t}},\,1\bigr)\rfloor-1.

Then ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt)=min⁡{1,C16​Ht​(dt+1)}\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})=\min\bigl\{1,\,\tfrac{C}{16H_{t}(d_{t}+1)}\bigr\} and ℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)≤exp⁡(−C)\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C)\leq\exp(-C) for every t∈[T]t\in[T].

Corollary 4.5 (Bernoulli scheduler)

Suppose σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}} is known. Let p=min⁡{1,C8​(σmax+1)}p=\min\bigl\{1,\,\tfrac{C}{8(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}+1)}\bigr\}, and for every t∈[T]t\in[T] let 𝔇t\mathfrak{D}_{t} be the two-point distribution on {−1,∞}\{-1,\infty\} with

ℙd′∼𝔇t​(d′=∞)=p,ℙd′∼𝔇t​(d′=−1)= 1−p.\textstyle\mathbb{P}_{d^{\prime}\sim\mathfrak{D}_{t}}(d^{\prime}=\infty)\;=\;p,\qquad\mathbb{P}_{d^{\prime}\sim\mathfrak{D}_{t}}(d^{\prime}=-1)\;=\;1-p.

Then ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt)=p\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})=p and ℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)≤exp⁡(−C)\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C)\leq\exp(-C) for every t∈[T]t\in[T].

The two corollaries sit at opposite ends of a tradeoff. Corollary 4.4 provides pt=O~​(Cdt+1)p_{t}=\tilde{O}(\tfrac{C}{d_{t}+1}), adapting to each round’s individual delay, while Corollary 4.5 achieves the uniform p=O⁡(Cσmax+1)p=O(\tfrac{C}{\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}+1}). Each is useful in different regimes, as the next section illustrates.

5 Regret Bounds for Capacity-Constrained OCO with Delayed Feedback

Combining the weighted regret bounds of Section 3 with the proxy-delay wrapper of Section 4 yields regret guarantees for capacity-constrained OCO and BCO under delayed feedback. The two theorems below cover the convex and strongly convex cases under first-order and bandit feedback, respectively, and constitute the main results of this work. The mild restriction C≥ln⁡T+1C\geq\ln T+1 ensures that the saturation probabilities of Lemma 4.3 sum to a constant over the horizon. The learning rates ηt\eta_{t} and smoothing parameters δt\delta_{t} depend on problem quantities that may not be known in advance: either dtotd_{\textnormal{tot}} and TT, or σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}. The former dependence can be removed by the two-dimensional doubling trick of [5], and the latter by a new doubling trick developed in Appendix F.

5.1Capacity-Constrained OCO with Delays

Suppose C≥ln⁡T+1C\geq\ln T+1, and consider 𝒲⁡(𝒜,𝔇)\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{A},\mathfrak{D}) (Algorithm 1), where 𝒜\mathcal{A} is DW-FTRL (1). With rates ηt=D/Gdtot+T\eta_{t}=\tfrac{D/G}{\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}+T}} and 𝔇\mathfrak{D} from Corollary 4.4, 𝒲⁡(𝒜,𝔇)\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{A},\mathfrak{D}) guarantees

R¯T​(x∗)=O⁡(G​D​dtot+T).\displaystyle\widebar{R}_{T}(x^{*})=O\left(GD\,{\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}+T}}\right).

Under λ\lambda-strong convexity (2.3), for rates ηt=1t​λ\eta_{t}=\frac{1}{t\lambda} and 𝔇\mathfrak{D} from Corollary 4.5, 𝒲⁡(𝒜,𝔇)\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{A},\mathfrak{D}) guarantees

R¯T​(x∗)=O⁡(G2λ​(σmax+1)​ln⁡T).\displaystyle\widebar{R}_{T}(x^{*})=O\left(\tfrac{G^{2}}{\lambda}(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}+1)\ln T\right).

To state the BCO bounds, we introduce the scale ratio ν=MG​r\nu=\frac{M}{Gr}, measuring the function-value scale relative to the Lipschitz scale G​rGr, where MM is the absolute value bound (Assumption 2.4).

5.2Capacity-Constrained BCO with Delays

Suppose C≥ln⁡T+1C\geq\ln T+1, and consider 𝒲⁡(𝒜,𝔇)\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{A},\mathfrak{D}), where 𝒜\mathcal{A} is DW-FTBL (2) and 𝔇\mathfrak{D} is from Corollary 4.5. With smoothing parameters δt=r​min⁡{1,ν​kt1/4​(1+σmaxC)1/4}\delta_{t}=r\,\min\left\{1,\,\tfrac{\sqrt{\nu k}}{t^{1/4}}\,(1+\tfrac{\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}}{C})^{1/4}\right\} and learning rates ηt=D/Gt1/2​σmax+(ν​kδt/r)2​(1+σmaxC)\eta_{t}=\tfrac{D/G}{t^{1/2}\sqrt{\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}+(\frac{\nu k}{\delta_{t}/r})^{2}(1+\frac{\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}}{C})}}, 𝒲⁡(𝒜,𝔇)\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{A},\mathfrak{D}) guarantees

R¯T​(x∗)=O⁡(G​D​(T​σmax+T3/4​(1+σmaxC)1/4​ν​k)).\displaystyle\widebar{R}_{T}(x^{*})=O\!\left(GD\left(\sqrt{T\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}}+T^{3/4}\left(1+\tfrac{\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}}{C}\right)^{1/4}\!\sqrt{\nu k}\right)\right).

Under λ\lambda-strong convexity (2.3), with ηt=1t​λ\eta_{t}=\tfrac{1}{t\lambda} and δt=r​min⁡{1,(ν2​k2​ln⁡(t+1)t)1/3​(1+σmaxC)1/3}\delta_{t}=r\,\min\left\{1,\,(\tfrac{\nu^{2}k^{2}\ln(t+1)}{t})^{1/3}({1+\tfrac{\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}}{C}})^{1/3}\right\},

R¯T​(x∗)=O⁡(G2λ​(σmax​ln⁡T+(T2​ln⁡T)1/3​(1+σmaxC)1/3​(ν​k)2/3)).\displaystyle\widebar{R}_{T}(x^{*})=O\!\Big(\tfrac{G^{2}}{\lambda}\Big(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\ln T+(T^{2}\ln T)^{1/3}(1+\tfrac{\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}}{C})^{1/3}(\nu k)^{2/3}\Big)\Big).

Both theorems follow from Theorem 4.1 by combining the weighted regret bounds of Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 with the saturation bounds of Corollaries 4.4 and 4.5; full proofs are deferred to Appendix E.

6 Discussion and Future Work

This work gives the first regret bounds for capacity-constrained OCO, in both first-order and bandit settings under convex and strongly convex losses. For first-order OCO, logarithmic capacity suffices to match unconstrained delayed rates; for BCO, capacity enters the dimension-dependent terms through powers of (1+σmax/C)(1+\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}/C).

Several directions remain open. First, our BCO bounds for convex losses scale as T​σmax\sqrt{T\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}} in the delay-dependent term rather than the optimal dtot\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}} of the unconstrained setting; closing this gap or establishing a separation is an open problem. Second, the capacity-constrained framework bears a structural resemblance to finite-buffer queueing systems, where jobs that find the buffer full are dropped. Our schedulers exploit this connection, but the precise relationship between queueing theory and online learning under capacity constraints warrants deeper exploration. Third, extending from oblivious to adaptive adversaries, who select losses and delays based on the player’s history, appears to require fundamentally new tools and is a compelling direction for future work.

Appendix A Additional Related Work

Comparison to [39].

The capacity-constrained framework was recently introduced by [39] for finite-action settings, specifically prediction with expert advice and multi-armed bandits. To manage the tracking set under the capacity limit, they developed a modular approach that decouples the observation scheduling policy from the base learning algorithm, proposing techniques such as batch partitioning and Pareto-distributed proxy delays. While we adopt their high-level separation of schedulers and base learners, extending this framework to continuous convex domains (OCO and BCO) introduces fundamentally new theoretical challenges. In particular, the proxy-delay scheduler of [39] inherently induces non-uniform observation probabilities; while discrete-action algorithms can absorb these via time-varying loss scales, such variable importance weights are highly detrimental to continuous bandit gradient estimation and strongly convex objectives. To address this, we introduce the delayed-weighted OCO and BCO framework, and design a novel unified proxy-delay scheduler calibrated to the maximum number of pending observations σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}} that yields the uniform importance weights necessary for our continuous-domain bounds. Furthermore, their preemptive scheduler requires prior knowledge of the maximum delay dmaxd_{\textnormal{max}} in the non-clairvoyant setting. In contrast, our approach accommodates a semi-clairvoyant model and removes the need for prior knowledge of delay bounds via the doubling trick.

Connections to online scheduling.

Our model is closely related to online job and interval scheduling [27, 51, 6, 35]. In online interval scheduling, jobs arrive sequentially with release times and processing intervals, and the algorithm must assign jobs to a bounded number of machines while respecting overlap constraints. Under the correspondence with our setting, rounds become jobs, tracking capacity corresponds to the number of available machines, and delays determine the durations for which machines remain occupied. Tracking a round occupies one unit of capacity until feedback arrives or the round is preempted. The quantity σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}} corresponds to the peak concurrency level of overlapping jobs, whereas dmaxd_{\textnormal{max}} reflects the longest processing duration and may therefore be much larger. This perspective helps explain regimes in which σmax≪dmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\ll d_{\textnormal{max}}, which naturally arise in queueing systems with moderate average load but heavy-tailed service times. The distinction between preemptive and non-preemptive schedulers in our framework also parallels classical scheduling models.

Connections to streaming algorithms.

Our framework also bears conceptual similarities to streaming algorithms [4, 32]. Streaming algorithms process massive data streams under strict memory constraints, typically maintaining compact randomized summaries or sketches rather than storing the entire stream. Analogously, in our setting the learner cannot retain all pending observations and must selectively track only a bounded subset of rounds. Both settings therefore rely on randomized sampling and compressed representations to preserve global performance guarantees despite limited resources. Classic examples include the AMS sketch [4], Count-Min Sketch [10], and HyperLogLog [13].

Online convex optimization.

Online convex optimization (OCO) and its feedback models have been studied extensively. Early work by [55] introduced online convex programming and established O⁡(T)O(\sqrt{T}) regret bounds for online gradient methods. For first-order feedback, subsequent research established the standard Θ⁡(T)\Theta(\sqrt{T}) minimax scaling for general convex losses (see, e.g., [1]). For λ\lambda-strongly convex losses, logarithmic regret is achievable; in particular, [16] provided O⁡(ln⁡T)O(\ln T) guarantees, which match the Ω⁡(ln⁡T)\Omega(\ln T) lower bound of [1]. Comprehensive background and further developments can be found in standard texts [18, 34].

Bandit convex optimization.

Bandit convex optimization (BCO) was initiated by [15], who introduced the classical single-point gradient estimator and obtained a regret of order O⁡(T3/4​k1/2)O(T^{3/4}k^{1/2}). Subsequently, [2] developed optimal algorithms for multi-point bandit feedback and sharpened the theoretical guarantees. For two-point feedback, they achieved O~​(T1/2​k2)\widetilde{O}(T^{1/2}k^{2}) regret for convex losses and O⁡(k2​ln⁡T)O(k^{2}\ln T) regret under strong convexity. For single-point feedback, they also demonstrated improved rates under additional curvature, including a T2/3T^{2/3}-type guarantee for strongly convex losses (specifically, O⁡((T2​ln⁡T)1/3​k2/3)O((T^{2}\ln T)^{1/3}k^{2/3}) up to problem-dependent constants). Complementary results for stochastic convex optimization under bandit feedback were established by [3]. For two-point feedback, [43] later introduced an optimal algorithm with an improved dimension dependence of O⁡(T1/2​k1/2)O(T^{1/2}k^{1/2}). A parallel line of work designs (nearly) minimax-optimal algorithms for general BCO that approach the Ω⁡(k​T)\Omega(k\sqrt{T}) lower bound of [42] (see, e.g., [8, 17, 24]). Because these methods typically incur prohibitive computational costs, exhibiting exponential or high-degree polynomial dependence on the dimension kk and/or the horizon TT, we refer the reader to [25] for a detailed treatment and further references.

Online convex optimization with delayed feedback.

Early investigations into online learning with delayed feedback date back to [50]. A systematic treatment of delayed-feedback online learning and reduction-style approaches was developed by [21], while [22] introduced a black-box reduction that processes feedback strictly in the order of its arrival. Beyond generic black-box techniques, a substantial body of literature focuses on algorithms explicitly tailored to delayed OCO (e.g., [54, 31, 38, 14, 47, 52, 49, 36]). Delayed BCO has similarly received dedicated attention, beginning with delayed extensions of bandit gradient methods [19] and advancing toward delay-adaptive bounds with improved delay dependence [5, 48]. Recently, [11] reduced delayed feedback to online learning with time-varying movement costs in the dynamic regret setting.

Delays in related sequential decision problems.

Delayed observations have been studied extensively in multi-armed bandits and related models (see, e.g., [9, 44, 5, 12, 29, 30, 37]). Such delays emerge naturally under resource limitations, including the capacity constraints we study [39]. Delayed feedback has additionally been explored in adversarial contextual bandits with general function approximation [26], as well as in reinforcement learning and Markov decision processes (MDPs) operating with delayed or asynchronous feedback (e.g., [7, 23, 20, 45, 41]).

We prove the regret bounds for DW-FTRL (Theorem 3.1) and DW-FTBL (Theorem 3.2) stated in Section 3. Both proofs follow the delayed-update template: we compare the actual iterates against a fictitious sequence that has access to all gradients without delay, and bound the drift between them using the stability lemma (Lemma B.4). In the bandit case, we control the variance of pending gradient estimators using a technique of [40] (Lemma C.1).

Lemma C.1

Under the conditions of Theorem 3.2, for every set ℬ⊆[T]\mathcal{B}\subseteq[T] with δ=mint∈ℬ⁡δt\delta=\min_{t\in\mathcal{B}}\delta_{t},

𝔼⁡[‖∑t∈ℬwt​g^t‖]≤2​(G​∑t∈ℬwt+kMδ​∑t∈ℬwt2).\displaystyle\E\!\left[\|\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}\widehat{g}_{t}\|\right]\leq 2\left(G\,\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}+\tfrac{kM}{\delta}\sqrt{\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}^{2}}\right).
Proof

For every t∈ℬt\in\mathcal{B}, let gt=∇ftδ​(ytδ)=𝔼⁡[g^t|ℱt]g_{t}=\nabla f^{\delta}_{t}(y^{\delta}_{t})=\E[\widehat{g}_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{t}] and note

‖gt‖≤Gand‖g^t‖≤k​Mδ.\displaystyle\|g_{t}\|\leq G\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\widehat{g}_{t}\|\leq\tfrac{kM}{\delta}.

Consequently, from the triangle inequality and Jensen’s inequality, it follows that

𝔼⁡[‖∑t∈ℬwt​g^t‖]\displaystyle\E\!\left[\|\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}\widehat{g}_{t}\|\right] ≤𝔼⁡[‖∑t∈ℬwt​gt‖]+𝔼⁡[‖∑t∈ℬwt​(g^t−gt)‖]\displaystyle\leq\E\!\left[\|\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}g_{t}\|\right]+\E\!\left[\|\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}(\widehat{g}_{t}-g_{t})\|\right]
≤G​∑t∈ℬwt+𝔼⁡[‖∑t∈ℬwt​(g^t−gt)‖2].\displaystyle\leq G\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}+\sqrt{\E\!\left[\|\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}(\widehat{g}_{t}-g_{t})\|^{2}\right]}.

The second term under the square root can bounded as

𝔼⁡[‖∑t∈ℬwt​(g^t−gt)‖2]\displaystyle\E\!\left[\|\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}(\widehat{g}_{t}-g_{t})\|^{2}\right] =𝔼⁡[∑t∈ℬwt2​‖g^t−gt‖2]\displaystyle=\E\!\left[\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}^{2}\|\widehat{g}_{t}-g_{t}\|^{2}\right]
+2​𝔼⁡[∑t=1T∑s=t+1T𝕀⁡(t,s∈ℬ)​⟨g^t−gt,g^s−gs⟩]\displaystyle+2\,\E\!\left[\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\textstyle\sum_{s=t+1}^{T}\mathbb{I}(t,s\in\mathcal{B})\,\langle{\widehat{g}_{t}-g_{t},\widehat{g}_{s}-g_{s}}\rangle\right]
≤∑t∈ℬwt2​(G+k​Mδ)2+0.\displaystyle\leq\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}^{2}(G+\tfrac{kM}{\delta})^{2}+0.

Combining these results, we write

𝔼⁡[‖∑t∈ℬwt​g^t‖]\displaystyle\E\!\left[\|\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}\widehat{g}_{t}\|\right] ≤G​∑t∈ℬwt+(G+k​Mδ)​∑t∈ℬwt2\displaystyle\leq G\,\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}+(G+\tfrac{kM}{\delta})\sqrt{\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}^{2}}
≤2​(G​∑t∈ℬwt+k​Mδ​∑t∈ℬwt2).\displaystyle\leq 2\left(G\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}+\tfrac{kM}{\delta}\sqrt{\textstyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}w_{t}^{2}}\right).

This concludes the proof of the lemma.

Appendix D Reduction via Proxy Delay Scheduling: Proofs

We prove the results of Section 4. The proof of Theorem 4.1 extends the importance-weighting argument of [39] from multi-armed bandits to the convex setting. The saturation bound (Lemma 4.3) and the Pareto scheduler (Corollary 4.4) simplify the corresponding analysis by reducing it to a single Chernoff condition on the tracking set size. The Bernoulli scheduler (Corollary 4.5), which calibrates to the maximum backlog σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}, is new to this work.

Theorem 4.1 (Restated) The weights forwarded to 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfy

wt=𝕀⁡(|𝒮t|<C)​𝕀​(dt′≥dt)ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt),𝔼⁡[wt]≤1,𝔼⁡[wt2]≤1ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt),𝔼⁡[wt​ws]≤1,w_{t}=\tfrac{\mathbb{I}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|<C)\,\mathbb{I}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})}{\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})},\quad\E[w_{t}]\leq 1,\quad\E[w_{t}^{2}]\leq\tfrac{1}{\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})},\quad\E[w_{t}w_{s}]\leq 1,

for all distinct t,s∈[T]t,s\in[T]. Moreover, the expected regret satisfies

R¯T​(u)≤𝔼⁡[∑t=1Twt​(ft​(xt)−ft​(u))]+GD​∑t=1Tℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C).\widebar{R}_{T}(u)\;\leq\;\E\!\left[\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}\bigl(f_{t}(x_{t})-f_{t}(u)\bigr)\right]+GD\,\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{P}\bigl(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C\bigr).
Proof

From the structure of Algorithm 1, feedback from round tt is observed in round t+dtt+d_{t} if and only if |𝒮t|<C|\mathcal{S}_{t}|<C and dt′≥dtd^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t}. Consequently, we have the identity wt=𝕀⁡(|𝒮t|<C)​𝕀​(dt′≥dt)ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt)w_{t}=\tfrac{\mathbb{I}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|<C)\,\mathbb{I}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})}{\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})}.

Therefore, for each t∈[T]t\in[T] and s∈[T]∖{t}s\in[T]\setminus\{t\}, it holds that

𝔼⁡[wt]≤𝔼⁡[𝕀⁡(dt′≥dt)ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt)]=1,𝔼⁡[wt2]≤𝔼⁡[𝕀⁡(dt′≥dt)(ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt))2]=1ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt),\displaystyle\E[w_{t}]\leq\E\left[\tfrac{\mathbb{I}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})}{\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})}\right]=1,\quad\E[w_{t}^{2}]\leq\E\left[\tfrac{\mathbb{I}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})}{(\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t}))^{2}}\right]=\tfrac{1}{\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})},
𝔼⁡[wt​ws]≤𝔼⁡[𝕀⁡(dt′≥dt)​𝕀​(ds′≥ds)ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt)​ℙ​(ds′≥ds)]=𝔼⁡[𝕀⁡(dt′≥dt)ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt)]​𝔼​[𝕀⁡(ds′≥ds)ℙ⁡(ds′≥ds)]=1,\displaystyle\E[w_{t}w_{s}]\leq\E\left[\tfrac{\mathbb{I}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})\,\mathbb{I}(d^{\prime}_{s}\geq d_{s})}{\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})\,\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{s}\geq d_{s})}\right]=\E\left[\tfrac{\mathbb{I}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})}{\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})}\right]\,\E\left[\tfrac{\mathbb{I}(d^{\prime}_{s}\geq d_{s})}{\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{s}\geq d_{s})}\right]=1,

where the last inequality applies the fact that proxy delays dt′d^{\prime}_{t} and ds′d^{\prime}_{s} are sampled independently.

For the regret bound, we write

R¯T​(u)\displaystyle\widebar{R}_{T}(u) =𝔼⁡[∑t=1T(ft​(xt)−ft​(u))]\displaystyle=\E\!\left[\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}(f_{t}(x_{t})-f_{t}(u))\right]
≤(a)𝔼⁡[∑t=1T𝕀⁡(|𝒮t|<C)​(ft​(xt)−ft​(u))]+GD​𝔼⁡[∑t=1T𝕀⁡(|𝒮t|=C)]\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(a)}}}{{\leq}}\E\!\left[\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{I}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|<C)\,(f_{t}(x_{t})-f_{t}(u))\right]+GD\,\E\!\left[\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{I}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C)\right]
=(b)𝔼⁡[∑t=1T𝕀⁡(|𝒮t|<C)​𝕀​(dt′≥dt)ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt)​(ft​(xt)−ft​(u))]+GD​∑t=1Tℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(b)}}}{{=}}\E\!\left[\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\tfrac{\mathbb{I}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|<C)\,\mathbb{I}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})}{\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})}\,(f_{t}(x_{t})-f_{t}(u))\right]+GD\,\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C)
=(c)𝔼⁡[∑t=1Twt​(ft​(xt)−ft​(u))]+GD​∑t=1Tℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C),\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(c)}}}{{=}}\E\!\left[\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}\,(f_{t}(x_{t})-f_{t}(u))\right]+GD\,\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C),

where (a) combines Assumptions 2.1 and 2.2, (b) uses the fact that dt′d^{\prime}_{t} is sampled from 𝔇t\mathfrak{D}_{t} at the start of round tt independently of StS_{t} and xtx_{t}, and (c) applies the identity wt=𝕀⁡(|𝒮t|<C)​𝕀​(dt′≥dt)ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt)w_{t}=\tfrac{\mathbb{I}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|<C)\,\mathbb{I}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})}{\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})}.

Lemma 4.3 (Restated) Consider proxy delay distributions 𝔇=(𝔇t)t=1T\mathfrak{D}=(\mathfrak{D}_{t})_{t=1}^{T} such that for every t∈[T]t\in[T]

∑s∈ℬt∪{t}ℙ⁡(ds′≥t−s)≤C8.\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}\cup\{t\}}\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{s}\geq t-s)\leq\frac{C}{8}.

Then, ℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)≤exp⁡(−C)\mathbb{P}\bigl(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C\bigr)\leq\exp(-C) for every t∈[T]t\in[T].

Proof

Fix t∈[T]t\in[T]. For each s∈ℬt∪{t}s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}\cup\{t\}, define Xs=𝕀⁡(ds′≥t−s)X_{s}=\mathbb{I}(d^{\prime}_{s}\geq t-s).

By independence of the proxy-delay draws across rounds, the random variables (Xs)s∈ℬt∪{t}(X_{s})_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}\cup\{t\}} are independent Bernoulli random variables. Moreover, by construction of the proxy scheduler, |𝒮t|≤∑s∈ℬt∪{t}Xs|\mathcal{S}_{t}|\leq\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}\cup\{t\}}X_{s}. Therefore, writing X=∑s∈ℬt∪{t}XsX=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}\cup\{t\}}X_{s}, we have

ℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)≤ℙ⁡(|𝒮t|≥C)≤ℙ⁡(X≥C).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C)\leq\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|\geq C)\leq\mathbb{P}(X\geq C).

Let μ=𝔼⁡[X]=∑s∈ℬt∪{t}ℙ⁡(ds′≥t−s)\mu=\E[X]=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}\cup\{t\}}\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{s}\geq t-s). By assumption, μ≤C/8\mu\leq C/8.

If μ=0\mu=0, then ℙ⁡(X≥C)=0\mathbb{P}(X\geq C)=0. Assume henceforth that μ>0\mu>0, and define

α=C/μ−1∈[7,∞).\displaystyle\alpha=C/\mu-1\in[7,\infty).

By the multiplicative Chernoff bound (e.g., see Theorem 2.3.1 from [46]),

ℙ⁡(X≥C)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(X\geq C) =ℙ⁡(X≥(1+α)​μ)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\bigl(X\geq(1+\alpha)\mu\bigr)
≤(eα(1+α)1+α)μ\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{e^{\alpha}}{(1+\alpha)^{1+\alpha}}\right)^{\mu}
=exp⁡(C⁡(α1+α−ln⁡(1+α))).\displaystyle=\exp\left(C\left(\tfrac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}-\ln(1+\alpha)\right)\right).

As the function f⁡(x)=ln⁡(1+x)−x1+xf(x)=\ln(1+x)-\frac{x}{1+x} is increasing on [0,∞)[0,\infty), α\alpha satisfies

α1+α−ln⁡(1+α)≤7/8−ln⁡8<−1.\displaystyle\tfrac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}-\ln(1+\alpha)\leq 7/8-\ln 8<-1.

Therefore,

ℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)≤ℙ⁡(X≥C)≤e−C.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigl(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C\bigr)\leq\mathbb{P}(X\geq C)\leq e^{-C}.

Corollary 4.4 (Restated) For each t∈[T]t\in[T], let Ht=∑j=1t1jH_{t}=\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{t}\tfrac{1}{j}. Take 𝔇t\mathfrak{D}_{t} to be the shifted floored Pareto distribution

𝔇t=⌊Pareto​(C16​Ht, 1)⌋−1.\mathfrak{D}_{t}\;=\;\lfloor\textnormal{Pareto}\bigl(\tfrac{C}{16H_{t}},\,1\bigr)\rfloor-1.

Then ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt)=min⁡{1,C16​Ht​(dt+1)}\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})=\min\bigl\{1,\,\tfrac{C}{16H_{t}(d_{t}+1)}\bigr\} and ℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)≤exp⁡(−C)\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C)\leq\exp(-C) for every t∈[T]t\in[T].

Proof

Fix t∈[T]t\in[T]. By the Pareto tail formula,

ℙ⁡(dt′≥t−s)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq t-s) =ℙ⁡(Pareto​(C16​Ht,1)≥t−s+1)=min⁡{1,C16​Ht​(t−s+1)}.\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\!\left(\textnormal{Pareto}\!\left(\tfrac{C}{16H_{t}},1\right)\geq t-s+1\right)=\min\left\{1,\tfrac{C}{16H_{t}(t-s+1)}\right\}.

It remains to verify the condition of Lemma 4.3. It follows from Fact B.2 for harmonic numbers.

Thus, Lemma 4.3 now yields ℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)≤e−C\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C)\leq e^{-C}.

Corollary 4.5 (Restated) Let p=min⁡{1,C8​(σmax+1)}p=\min\{1,\tfrac{C}{8(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}+1)}\}. For every t∈[T]t\in[T], let the proxy distribution 𝔇t∈Δ⁡({−1,∞})\mathfrak{D}_{t}\in\Delta(\{-1,\infty\}) be given by

ℙd′∼𝔇t​(d′=∞)=p,ℙd′∼𝔇t​(d′=−1)=1−p.\displaystyle\textstyle\mathbb{P}_{d^{\prime}\sim\mathfrak{D}_{t}}(d^{\prime}=\infty)=p,\qquad\mathbb{P}_{d^{\prime}\sim\mathfrak{D}_{t}}(d^{\prime}=-1)=1-p.

Then, ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt)=p\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})=p and ℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)≤exp⁡(−C)\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C)\leq\exp(-C) for every t∈[T]t\in[T].

Proof

Fix t∈[T]t\in[T]. Since dt≥0d_{t}\geq 0 and dt′∈{−1,∞}d^{\prime}_{t}\in\{-1,\infty\}, ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt)=ℙ⁡(dt′=∞)=p\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})=\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}=\infty)=p.

Thus, the condition of Lemma 4.3 is satisfied

∑s∈ℬt∪{t}ℙ⁡(ds′≥t−s)=p​|ℬt∪{t}|=p⁡(σt+1)≤C⁡(σt+1)8​(σmax+1)≤C/8.\displaystyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}\cup\{t\}}\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{s}\geq t-s)=p\,|\mathcal{B}_{t}\cup\{t\}|=p(\sigma_{t}+1)\leq\tfrac{C(\sigma_{t}+1)}{8(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}+1)}\leq C/8.

Applying Lemma 4.3, we obtain

ℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)≤exp⁡(−C).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C)\leq\exp(-C).

This completes the proof.

Appendix E Guarantees for Capacity-Constrained OCO and BCO: Proofs

In this section, we prove the main regret bounds for capacity-constrained OCO and BCO stated in Section 5, covering both convex and strongly convex losses.

Theorem 5.1 (Restated) Suppose C≥ln⁡T+1C\geq\ln T+1, and consider 𝒲⁡(𝒜,𝔇)\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{A},\mathfrak{D}), where 𝒜\mathcal{A} is DW-FTRL (1). With learning rates ηt=D/Gdtot+T\eta_{t}=\tfrac{D/G}{\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}+T}} and 𝔇\mathfrak{D} from Corollary 4.4, 𝒲⁡(𝒜,𝔇)\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{A},\mathfrak{D}) guarantees

R¯T​(x∗)=O⁡(G​D​dtot+T).\displaystyle\widebar{R}_{T}(x^{*})=O\left(GD\,{\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}+T}}\right).

Under λ\lambda-strong convexity (2.3), for rates ηt=1t​λ\eta_{t}=\frac{1}{t\lambda} and 𝔇\mathfrak{D} from Corollary 4.5, 𝒲⁡(𝒜,𝔇)\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{A},\mathfrak{D}) guarantees

R¯T​(x∗)=O⁡(G2λ​(σmax+1)​ln⁡T).\displaystyle\widebar{R}_{T}(x^{*})=O\left(\tfrac{G^{2}}{\lambda}(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}+1)\ln T\right).

Note that C≥ln⁡(e​T)≥∑t=1T1t=HTC\geq\ln(eT)\geq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1}{t}=H_{T} and T​e−C≤1Te^{-C}\leq 1 throughout the proof. Fix comparator u∈𝒦u\in\mathcal{K}. We prove the bounds on R¯T​(u)\widebar{R}_{T}(u) for general convex and strongly convex losses separately.

General convex losses: We use fixed learning rate ηt=η\eta_{t}=\eta for the value η=D/Gdtot+T\eta=\tfrac{D/G}{\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}+T}}. Combining Theorems 4.1, 3.1 and Corollary 4.4, we write

R¯T​(u)\displaystyle\widebar{R}_{T}(u) ≤𝔼⁡[∑t=1Twt​(ft​(xt)−ft​(u))]+GD​∑t=1Tℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)\displaystyle\leq\E\!\left[\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}(f_{t}(x_{t})-f_{t}(u))\right]+GD\,\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C)
≤D2η+G2​η​𝔼⁡[∑t=1T(wt2+wt​∑s∈ℬtws)]+GD​T​exp⁡(−C)\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{D^{2}}{\eta}+G^{2}\eta\,\E\!\left[\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}(w_{t}^{2}+w_{t}\textstyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}w_{s})\right]+GD\,T\exp(-C)
≤D2η+G2​η​∑t=1T(max⁡{1,16​HtC​(dt+1)}+σt)+G​D\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{D^{2}}{\eta}+G^{2}\eta\,\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\max\left\{1,\tfrac{16H_{t}}{C}\,(d_{t}+1)\right\}+\sigma_{t}\right)+GD
≤(a)D2η+G2​η​(1+16​HTC)​(dtot+T)+G​D\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(a)}}}{{\leq}}\tfrac{D^{2}}{\eta}+G^{2}\eta\,\left(1+\tfrac{16H_{T}}{C}\right)\,\left(d_{\textnormal{tot}}+T\right)+GD
≤(b)D2η+17​G2​η​(dtot+T)+G​D\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(b)}}}{{\leq}}\tfrac{D^{2}}{\eta}+17G^{2}\eta\,\left(d_{\textnormal{tot}}+T\right)+GD
=18​G​D​dtot+T+G​D,\displaystyle=18GD\,\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}+T}+GD,

where (a) applies ∑t=1Tσt=dtot\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sigma_{t}=d_{\textnormal{tot}} from Lemma 2.6 and (b) follows for C≥HTC\geq H_{T}.

R¯T​(u)\displaystyle\widebar{R}_{T}(u) ≤𝔼⁡[∑t=1Twt​(ft​(xt)−ft​(u))]+GD​∑t=1Tℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)\displaystyle\leq\E\!\left[\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}(f_{t}(x_{t})-f_{t}(u))\right]+GD\,\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C)

≤(b)2​G2λ​∑t=1Tℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(b)}}}{{\leq}}\tfrac{2G^{2}}{\lambda}\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C)
≤2​G2λ​T​e−C\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{2G^{2}}{\lambda}\,Te^{-C}

where (a) uses the fact that dt′d^{\prime}_{t} is sampled independently of xtx_{t}, and (b) lets D≤2​GλD\leq\frac{2G}{\lambda} (see Fact B.1).

For the second term in (4), we apply 𝔼⁡[wt2]≤1p\E[w_{t}^{2}]\leq\frac{1}{p} and 𝔼⁡[ws​wt]≤1\E[w_{s}w_{t}]\leq 1 from Theorem 4.1 for p=min⁡{1,C8​(σmax+1)}p=\min\{1,\frac{C}{8(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}+1)}\} in Corollary 4.5 and substitute learning rate values ηt=1t​λ\eta_{t}=\frac{1}{t\lambda},

Appendix F Doubling Trick over Maximum Backlog

The strongly convex and bandit results of Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 require tuning with knowledge of σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}, which may not be available in advance. Since the learning rates and smoothing parameters in all our results depend on the round index tt but not on the horizon TT, our base algorithms are anytime in TT, and we need only double over σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}. This avoids the two-dimensional doubling over (T,dtot)(T,d_{\textnormal{tot}}) used by [5].

Epoch structure.

Define backlog guesses Sj=2j−1S_{j}=2^{j}-1 for j∈ℤ≥0j\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. The wrapper initializes at epoch j=0j=0 and restarts the base algorithm with parameters tuned to maximum backlog SjS_{j}. Within each epoch, the algorithm runs until the observed backlog exceeds SjS_{j}, at which point the epoch ends, jj is incremented, and the algorithm restarts with the updated guess. Upon starting a new epoch, the wrapper clears the tracking set, discarding any pending observations from the previous epoch. The final epoch index is J=⌈log2⁡(σmax+1)⌉J=\lceil\,{\log_{2}(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}+1)}\,\rceil.

F.1Doubling over σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}

Suppose the base algorithm is anytime in TT: for any backlog guess S~\widetilde{S}, on any interval of length T′T^{\prime} with maximum backlog at most S~\widetilde{S}, it guarantees regret at most

R⁡(T′,S~)≤φ0​(T′)+∑m=1Mφm​(T′)​(S~+1)bm,\displaystyle R(T^{\prime},\widetilde{S})\;\leq\;\varphi_{0}(T^{\prime})+\textstyle\sum_{m=1}^{M}\varphi_{m}(T^{\prime})\,(\widetilde{S}+1)^{b_{m}},

where bm>0b_{m}>0 and each φm:ℕ→[0,∞)\varphi_{m}:\mathbb{N}\to[0,\infty) for m∈{0}∪[M]m\in\{0\}\cup[M] is non-decreasing. Then the doubling wrapper guarantees

R⁡(T,σmax)=O⁡(φ0​(T)​log⁡(σmax+1)+∑m=1Mφm​(T)​(σmax+1)bm).\displaystyle R(T,\sigma_{\textnormal{max}})\;=\;O\!\left(\varphi_{0}(T)\log(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\!+\!1)+\textstyle\sum_{m=1}^{M}\varphi_{m}(T)\,(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}+1)^{b_{m}}\right).
Proof

The wrapper produces at most J+1J+1 epochs, indexed j=0,1,…,Jj=0,1,\ldots,J with J=⌈log2⁡(σmax+1)⌉J=\lceil\,{\log_{2}(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}+1)}\,\rceil. Let LjL_{j} denote the number of rounds in epoch jj. Since Lj≤TL_{j}\leq T and each φm\varphi_{m} is non-decreasing, the regret decomposes as

R⁡(T,σmax)≤∑j=0JR⁡(Lj,Sj)≤(J+1)​φ0​(T)+∑m=1Mφm​(T)​∑j=0J2bm​j.\displaystyle R(T,\sigma_{\textnormal{max}})\;\leq\;\textstyle\sum_{j=0}^{J}R(L_{j},S_{j})\;\leq\;(J\!+\!1)\,\varphi_{0}(T)\;+\;\textstyle\sum_{m=1}^{M}\varphi_{m}(T)\textstyle\sum_{j=0}^{J}2^{b_{m}j}.

The first term equals O⁡(φ0​(T)​log⁡(σmax+1))O(\varphi_{0}(T)\log(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}+1)). For the second, since bm>0b_{m}>0, the geometric series satisfies ∑j=0J2bm​j=O⁡((σmax+1)bm)\textstyle\sum_{j=0}^{J}2^{b_{m}j}=O\big((\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}+1)^{b_{m}}\big). Summing over m∈[M]m\in[M] completes the proof.

Remark F.2

Every term in the regret bounds of Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 that depends on σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}} has bm>0b_{m}>0, so the geometric series absorbs the epoch count for these terms. The σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}-independent terms (captured by φ0\varphi_{0}) incur a log⁡(σmax+1)\log(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}+1) overhead because, unlike dtotd_{\textnormal{tot}} or TT, the maximum backlog does not accumulate across epochs: each restart effectively begins a new game, and φ0\varphi_{0} is charged in full for every epoch. The general convex OCO bound of Theorem 5.1 does not depend on σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}; for it, we use the doubling trick of [5] over TT and dtotd_{\textnormal{tot}} instead.

Appendix G Non-Preemptive Framework

[39] also studied a more restrictive variant of capacity-constrained online learning in which preemption is disallowed: once a round enters the tracking set 𝒮\mathcal{S}, it must remain until its feedback arrives. Our framework recovers this variant by restricting the support of proxy delay distributions 𝔇t\mathfrak{D}_{t} to {−1,∞}\{-1,\infty\} (Section 4), so that each round is either rejected outright (dt′=−1d^{\prime}_{t}=-1) or committed to until feedback delivery (dt′=∞d^{\prime}_{t}=\infty). The two-point schedulers in Corollaries 4.5 and G.1 are non-preemptive in this sense.

Corollary G.1

Assume the framework is clairvoyant. For each t∈[T]t\in[T], define Ht=∑j=1t1jH_{t}=\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{t}\frac{1}{j} and pt=min⁡{1,C16​Ht​(dt+1)}p_{t}=\min\left\{1,\tfrac{C}{16H_{t}(d_{t}+1)}\right\}. Let the proxy distribution 𝔇t∈Δ⁡({−1,∞})\mathfrak{D}_{t}\in\Delta(\{-1,\infty\}) be given by

ℙd′∼𝔇t​(d′=∞)=pt,ℙd′∼𝔇t​(d′=−1)=1−pt.\displaystyle\textstyle\mathbb{P}_{d^{\prime}\sim\mathfrak{D}_{t}}(d^{\prime}=\infty)=p_{t},\qquad\mathbb{P}_{d^{\prime}\sim\mathfrak{D}_{t}}(d^{\prime}=-1)=1-p_{t}.

Then, ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt)=pt\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})=p_{t} and ℙ⁡(|𝒮t|=C)≤exp⁡(−C)\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{S}_{t}|=C)\leq\exp(-C) for every t∈[T]t\in[T].

Proof

Fix t∈[T]t\in[T]. Since 𝔇t∈Δ⁡({−1,∞})\mathfrak{D}_{t}\in\Delta(\{-1,\infty\}) and dt∈ℤ≥0d_{t}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, we immediately have ℙ⁡(dt′≥dt)=ℙ⁡(dt′=∞)=pt\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}\geq d_{t})=\mathbb{P}(d^{\prime}_{t}=\infty)=p_{t}. The rest follows analogously to the proof of Corollary 4.4.

Since both schedulers satisfy the same saturation and weight moment bounds as their preemptive counterparts, combining them with the analysis of Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 yields identical regret guarantees in the non-preemptive setting.
